prompt:
There are several musical treats across genres to enjoy this week in Ottawa clubs (and churches).
From Oakland, California comes SWMRS, a group of young men who already have several albums under the belt, albeit under different names. With their new moniker, they now offer punk-informed surf rock, having in their “older years” ditched the rapid guitar of their indie punk days for a more laid back vibe, albeit still with some teen angst; Miley is a punk rock queen comes to mind.
If they sound more acccomplished than one might think (and with slightly familiar sound), that might be because they have real rockstar pedigree and assistance: one of them calls Green Day’s frontman Billy Joe dad.
But that should not to dismiss the band’s own party draw, which has them selling out shows on their current U.S. tour, with this one of only four stops in Canada — though it does not appear on their official tour schedule. With The Frights, The Boreds, March 10, 8:30 p.m., Zaphod’s. $10 at the door. spectrasonic.com
Folk superstar Judy Collins, at the age of 76, is still wowing audiences with her own brand of vulnerable, inviting singing, performing over 100 shows a year and touring annually. She is back in Ottawa on one of her rare stops, performing at the sweet-sounding. intimate space of Southminster United Church. She has a new album, returning to her roots of picking great songs from the best composers, but this time the album is a series of duets with suitably famous partners, though we do not think she is bringing Willie Nelson along with her. She is being joined by other folk-singing charmer Garnet Rogers, though. March 11, 8 p.m., 15 Aylmer Ave. $46.50. folkzone.ca
Tech noire music and visual producer Dada Pogrom, otherwise known as Ottawa-raised Kenny Balys, is returning after several years travelling between Iceland and Toronto with a new batch of eclectic, visually-studded songs to play at the House of Targ’s latest Switched on Synths night.
With that name, and the preference for minimalism, minor chords and challenging subject, his’ music at first glance might seem dark, but it all comes with a danceable, pop beat and Balys confesses he really just wants the audience to have fun. (The dark periods of history echoed in his group’s name was a fluke, after all, created in a moment with a Petit Larousse and a fork.)
Look for his beloved vintage technology, that was once an embarrassment and now has a certain cachet (and that he could sell for some good profit if he were not so married to the 80s synth-pop sound of groups like Rational Youth). His show will also come with the expected visuals, though there are more to be had on his new creation, a combined video-audio piece of art not yet released, but that will be available for purchase at the show. With Automelodi, Hard Science, March11, 10 p.m., House of Targ. $10 in advance. www.houseoftarg.com
Rock fans of the big, the retro, the songs that demand you sing along will get great pleasure out of The Sheepdogs show at Bronson Centre, featuring tunes off their most recent, fifth album, Future Nostalgia. They set out to create “pure, simple good time music” and have done so, with tunes such as I’m Gonna Be Myself and the familiarity of Downtown’s guitars and echoing chorus. This will be the album to take with you on that road trip, the month at the cottage or your next BBQ on the back porch — and the show to urge spring on its way. with Beat Cops, March 11, 8 p.m., Bronson Centre. $32.50. spectrasonic.com
Nova Scotia rapper Classified hits the Algonquin Commons theatre on tour with his new album, Greatful, that had a little collaboration from such as Snoop Dogg, David Myles and the scratchy-scratch of DJ Premier. He enjoyed a certain mainstream acclaim with his last album, notably for Inner Ninja, which won him two Juno Awards. It may be that success or mere age and fatherhood creeping up, but the anger of his early stuff has waned for a more radio-friendly sound. But don’t worry, he is still witty, political (check out Work Away) and letting listeners in on the joke. with SonReal, hip hop, 8 p.m., Algonquin Commons Theatre. $30-$35.
British folkish, punkish disco sort Frank Turner and his band the Sleeping Souls are enough of a draw on their own. Turner’s songs are known to be raw and, with his 2015 album Positive Songs For Negative People, full of joie de vivre and beauty (see the moving Song for Josh). These are not milquetoast tunes to ignore in the background; they will make you dance or cry.
However, he is joined by the ever-charming folk-pop singer songwriter Mo Kenney who we do not see enough of in Ottawa. She was last in town about a year ago, when she sold out at the NAC. From Nova Scotia, she is becoming everything her mentor Joel Plaskett saw in her, including the ability to captivate with just that evocative voice, playing folk with a modern, 60s sensibility. Her sophomore album In My Dream, with the catchy earworm Telephone we have still no desire to get out of our head, has been nominated for a Juno Award. March 12, with Northcote, 7 p.m., Bronson Centre. $35. spectrasonic.com
“Have you ever seen Animal House?” Frat rock, that beer-infused soul blues music played in fraternity houses of the 50s and 60s is what will happen when Fuad and the Feztones take to the stage at Irene’s. It’s a “silly concept band,” created by the founders of the 80s garage group The Gruesomes, says member John Davis, allowing them to play music popularized by such as The Kingsmen and The Wailers, wear letter sweaters and fez hats, give themselves “Cairo”-based alter egos and write songs such as Beeramid and Djibouti Call.
Now with jobs and families, they play where they want to and Irene’s remains one of their favourites, turning down other offers in Toronto as “too far away” — most of the band are based in Montreal. The shows always sell out and, Davis says, anyone who shows up in a toga will get a prize. with The Separatwists, March 12, 9 p.m., Irene’s Pub. $10. irenespub.ca
Being Sunday, and therefore a bit incongruous, there is a loud, aggressive, all-ages alt-rock show on at Mavericks, featuring the atmosphere “sex rock” of Sycamour, known for their beautiful vocals over lots of raging guitar and drums. They play with a roster of varying levels of hardcore rock and metal acts, including Brightwell, Projekt F, Wkfld, Greylights, Footsteps to Gaia. March 13, 7 p.m., Mavericks. www.mavericksbar.com
For something different, historical and (yet!) fun: award-winning banjoist Jayme Stone has been reviving and reimagining some of the music collected by folklorist and sound recording pioneer Alan Lomax with the help of some varied roots musicians. We’re talking Appalachian ballads, sea chanties from the Bahamas, songs touching on the universal of human experience sung by homemakers to sea captains, to children and over meals gathered from around the world. At this performance of his The Lomax Project, Stone will be joined by Moira Smiley, Sumaia Jackson and Joe Phillips. March 16, 7:30 p.m., NAC Fourth Stage. $35. nac-cna.ca
NB: MonkeyJunk have two shows at the end of the month at The Black Sheep Inn. Their shows regularly sell out but, as of press time, there seemed to still be some still available.

The Most Perfectly Succulent Eye of Round Roast (that tastes like Prime Rib, only better)
I really think one of the keys to this roast is covering this bad boy in salt and letting it marinate for 18-24 hours before you cook it. It helps to flavor the meat to ridiculously glorious levels and the salt also helps to break down this tougher cut, insuring SUCCULENCE that would drive any meat lover mad with love.
Ingredients:
Boneless eye round roast (about 4 pounds)
4 tsp kosher salt
2 tsp canola oil plus 1 tablespoon
2 tsp ground black pepper
Directions:
1. Cover roast evenly with salt. Rub into the skin and all around. If your roast is larger, use more salt. This step is crucial. This will help to break down the meat, insuring its ‘melt in your mouthiness’. Toss the roast into a Ziploc bag or if it’s too big, wrap it in plastic wrap. Refrigerate for 18-24 hours. The longer the better.
2. Take the roast out of the refrigerator, place it in a shallow roasting pan. Allow to sit at room temperature for 30 minutes. Meanwhile, position your oven rack into the middle of the oven and preheat to 225 degrees.
3. In a large skillet, heat 1 tablespoon of canola oil over medium high heat. While the oil is getting hot, drizzle the roast with 2 tsp of canola oil and season with pepper. Using tongs, place your roast into the skillet and sear on all sides (until brown and glistening), about 4 minutes per side for a total of 16 minutes. Return the roast to the shallow roasting pan.
4. Cook the roast in the 225 degree oven until an instant read thermometer inserted into the center of the roast registers 115 degrees for medium rare (about 1.5 hours) OR 125 degrees for medium (about 2 hours).
5. Turn off the oven, BUT LEAVE THE ROAST INSIDE for another 50 minutes longer (for a medium roast – 30 minutes for rare). At the end of the 50 minutes, allow to rest for 20 minutes. Transfer to a carving board and slice thinly against the grain (crosswise), and serve.
*** My roast was 3.92 pounds. Cooking times may vary. Though...you could certainly cook your roast longer, to 2.25 hours but remember though the meat will be cooked more, this cut of meat will turn chewy if you cook it too high, too long, and without the benefit of the salt break down.
